summary:
We propose the Danakil Depression in Ethiopia, and specifically the Dallol hydrothermal field, as an under-used Earth analog for acidic, salt-rich Mars such as Meridiani Planum, where NASA's Opportunity rover found sulfate-rich rocks formed in acidic, salty water. Most analog work uses cold deserts and craters like Atacama, Antarctica and Haughton Crater, which match Mars' climate but not this chemistry.

We built an open, reproducible Python notebook that compares terrain fairly: it computes median slope from NASA's MGS MOLA 463 m Mars elevation map and ESA's Copernicus GLO-30 Earth elevation data, averaged to the same 463 m pixels. We then combine seven factors into a transparent similarity index with two weightings. Dallol scores 0.72 for geochemistry science and 0.46 for field operations: a strong mineral and water-chemistry analog, and a weak climate analog. At Mars-map scale it is also the flattest site we tested (0.03° vs Meridiani's 0.26°).

This helps mission teams choose where to test instruments, practise biosignature searches and rank Mars landing sites.
details: WHAT IT DOES Project Red Shift identifies and characterises the Danakil Depression (Dallol, Ethiopia) as a terrestrial analog for acidic, salt-rich Mars, such as Meridiani Planum. It uses open NASA and ESA data to measure how similar the two places are, factor by factor, and shows clearly where the analogy is strong and where it breaks down. HOW IT WORKS 1. Terrain: A Jupyter notebook downloads NASA's MGS MOLA 463 m global Mars elevation map and ESA's Copernicus GLO-30 Earth elevation data for Dallol and three well-known analogs (Atacama, Haughton Crater, Death Valley). Because slope depends strongly on pixel size, Earth data is averaged to the same ~463 m pixels as MOLA, and Mars distances use Mars' own radius (3,396 km). It then computes the median slope in a 20 km box at each site. 2. Similarity index: A Python script scores seven factors from 0 to 1 (mineralogy, acidic-brine history, terrain, temperature, atmosphere, gravity, radiation) and combines them with two weight sets: one for geochemistry science and one for field operations. 3. Sensitivity check: The script tests how much the result changes when the scoring scales change. RESULTS - Dallol is the flattest site at Mars-map scale: median slope 0.03° vs 0.26° at Meridiani, while Atacama, Haughton Crater and Death Valley are 2.1–3.9°. Terrain score: 0.96. - Geochemistry-weighted similarity: 0.72. Operations-weighted similarity: 0.46. - The result is robust: changing the scoring scales moves the indices only between 0.69–0.73 and 0.43–0.52. BENEFITS AND IMPACT Dallol is one of the few places on Earth with active, extremely acidic, hypersaline water and fresh salt and sulfate deposits, the kind of environment that shaped Meridiani Planum. It can help teams test Raman, XRD and infrared instruments on real sulfates, practise biosignature searches in extreme brines, learn which evaporites form and survive (to help rank landing sites), and stress-test robots in heat, salt and remote conditions. WHERE THE ANALOGY BREAKS Dallol is hot (about 34 °C vs about −60 °C), under thick air (1013 vs 6 mbar), at full Earth gravity, with low radiation. Our index shows these differences clearly, and we recommend pairing Dallol with a cold-desert analog such as Antarctica's Dry Valleys. WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE Instead of looking for a place that "looks like Mars," we chose an under-studied site for its chemistry, compared terrain at matched resolution so the comparison is fair, and built a transparent index whose weighting shows that "how good an analog" depends on the mission goal. TOOLS Python, Jupyter / Google Colab, rasterio (GDAL), NumPy, pandas, matplotlib, Git and GitHub. The whole analysis runs in one click from our repository: https://github.com/mehradjroshani-cpu/danakil-mars-analog LIMITATIONS AND NEXT STEPS Slope is computed from elevation data. Temperature, pressure, gravity and radiation use approximate literature values, and the mineralogy and brine-history scores are expert judgement for now. Next we will add measured temperatures (NASA MODIS land surface temperature vs Mars THEMIS), map sulfates with ASTER vs CRISM to replace the judgement scores, and run the same index over other salt basins to find more hidden analogs.
